course.title: Network Traffic Analysis
course.description: A practical, analyst-focused course for learning how to capture, decode, filter, summarize, and investigate network traffic. Students progress from packet and protocol fundamentals through TCP/IP behavior, DNS/HTTP/TLS analysis, packet capture with Wireshark and TShark, network telemetry with Zeek and Suricata, flow analysis, detection engineering, encrypted-traffic reasoning, threat hunting, and repeatable incident investigations. The course emphasizes evidence-driven analysis, safe lab practice, time normalization, baselining, false-positive control, and production-minded workflows.
prerequisites: Basic computer and command-line skills (Windows PowerShell or a Unix-like shell).
Basic networking concepts: IP addresses, ports, DNS, TCP/UDP, and the OSI/TCP-IP model.
A lab environment where packet captures can be analyzed safely and legally.
Optional but helpful: basic Python for automating text/JSON analysis.
learningOutcomes: Explain how Ethernet, IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, DNS, HTTP, and TLS behaviors appear in packet captures.
Capture and filter traffic safely with Wireshark and TShark using both capture and display filters.
Reconstruct TCP conversations and interpret connection setup, retransmissions, resets, and termination.
Analyze DNS, HTTP, TLS, QUIC, and common application-layer indicators without relying on payload alone.
Use Zeek logs and Suricata EVE JSON as structured network-security telemetry.
Analyze flow records and distinguish volume, duration, directionality, periodicity, and scan-like behavior.
Build and tune network detections using evidence, context, thresholds, and false-positive analysis.
Reason about encrypted traffic using metadata, protocol handshakes, timing, destinations, and certificate context.
Perform a defensible network investigation from initial signal to hypothesis, evidence, conclusion, and documented timeline.
Automate repeatable network-triage tasks with Python while preserving data provenance and analyst traceability.

modules.title: Traffic Analysis Foundations
modules.description: Establish the evidence model, collection architecture, and safe operating practices required for defensible network analysis.

lessons.title: What Network Traffic Analysis Is
lessons.description: Define the analyst’s role, telemetry types, and the distinction between packets, flows, logs, and alerts.
learningObjectives: Explain what network traffic analysis measures and what it cannot prove by itself.
Distinguish packet captures, flow records, protocol logs, and IDS alerts.

notes.text: Network traffic analysis is the disciplined interpretation of communications observed between systems. A packet capture preserves wire-level details; a flow record compresses conversations into metadata; Zeek and IDS logs add structured interpretation. Analysts should treat each source as evidence with different resolution, cost, and blind spots.

items: Packet capture: strongest detail, largest volume, payload may be unavailable or encrypted.
Flow telemetry: excellent for who/when/how much, weak for application content.
Alerts: fast signal but may be noisy and rule-dependent.
Context sources—asset inventory, identity, DNS, endpoint telemetry—often determine whether network evidence is meaningful.

quiz.question: Which source normally preserves the greatest amount of wire-level detail?
quiz.answer: Packet capture
quiz.explanation: A packet capture can retain headers and, when available, payload bytes; flow and alert data are derived summaries.

summary: Network traffic analysis is the disciplined interpretation of communications observed between systems. A packet capture preserves wire-level details; a flow record compresses conversations into metadata; Zeek and IDS logs add structured interpretation. Analysts should treat each source as evidence with different resolution, cost, and blind spots.

lessons.title: Observation Points and Collection Architecture
lessons.description: Understand where traffic can be observed: endpoints, taps, SPAN/mirror ports, gateways, cloud flow logs, and sensors.
learningObjectives: Compare common traffic observation points and their trade-offs.
Select a collection point appropriate to a stated investigative question.

notes.text: Visibility depends on placement. A sensor at an internet edge sees north-south traffic but may miss east-west traffic inside a flat network. A mirror port can duplicate selected switch traffic, while a physical or virtual tap can provide dedicated monitoring paths. Cloud environments often expose metadata through provider flow logs rather than raw packets.

items: Ask what traffic path contains the evidence before collecting.
Document the observation point, interface, VLAN/VPC/subnet, and capture filters.
Treat dropped packets and sampling as explicit limitations.

quiz.question: An analyst needs visibility into east-west traffic between internal application servers. Which placement is most directly aligned?
options: Internal network sensor at a mirror/tap point
quiz.answer: Internal network sensor at a mirror/tap point
quiz.explanation: East-west traffic stays inside the environment, so an internal observation point is required.

summary: Visibility depends on placement. A sensor at an internet edge sees north-south traffic but may miss east-west traffic inside a flat network. A mirror port can duplicate selected switch traffic, while a physical or virtual tap can provide dedicated monitoring paths. Cloud environments often expose metadata through provider flow logs rather than raw packets.

lessons.title: Packet, Flow, and Session Semantics
lessons.description: Build the vocabulary needed to discuss network evidence precisely.
learningObjectives: Define packet, segment, datagram, flow, session, and transaction in practical terms.
Explain why the same event can look different across telemetry layers.

notes.text: A packet is an IP-layer unit; TCP commonly carries a byte stream in segments, while UDP transports datagrams. A flow typically groups traffic by a tuple such as source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol, and a time window. A session is an application or protocol interaction whose boundaries may not map cleanly to one flow.

Example flow key (conceptual):
(src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port, protocol)

quiz.question: Why can one application session produce multiple network flows?
options: Because flows may be grouped by different 5-tuples or connection lifetimes
quiz.answer: Because flows may be grouped by different 5-tuples or connection lifetimes
quiz.explanation: Applications often open multiple connections, and flow records are typically scoped to specific transport tuples and time windows.

summary: A packet is an IP-layer unit; TCP commonly carries a byte stream in segments, while UDP transports datagrams. A flow typically groups traffic by a tuple such as source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol, and a time window. A session is an application or protocol interaction whose boundaries may not map cleanly to one flow.

lessons.title: Ethical and Safe Lab Practice
lessons.description: Set boundaries for capture, storage, sharing, and handling of potentially sensitive traffic.
learningObjectives: Identify legal and organizational authorization requirements before capture.
Apply safe handling practices to packet captures and extracted artifacts.

notes.text: Only capture and analyze traffic you are authorized to inspect. Packet captures can contain credentials, tokens, personal data, and confidential business information.

items: Use isolated labs or explicitly authorized production collection.
Minimize collection when the investigative question does not require full payloads.
Restrict access and document retention for captures.
When sharing samples for training, sanitize sensitive content and preserve the original evidence separately.

quiz.question: Why is a packet capture more sensitive than a simple flow summary?
options: It can contain application payloads and secrets
quiz.answer: It can contain application payloads and secrets
quiz.explanation: Payloads can expose credentials, tokens, documents, or personal data that a basic flow record does not retain.

summary: Set boundaries for capture, storage, sharing, and handling of potentially sensitive traffic.

tasks.title: Choose the Right Evidence Source
tasks.description: Select the minimum useful telemetry for three investigative questions.
tasks.problemStatement: For each scenario—port scan, large file transfer, and DNS-based suspicious domain activity—choose packet, flow, DNS log, Zeek log, or IDS telemetry and justify the choice.
objectives: Match investigative questions to telemetry types.
State known blind spots and collection assumptions.
requirements: A written answer table; course concepts from Module 1.
tasks.hint: Start from the question: content, volume, protocol behavior, or alert context?
tasks.solutionCode: Scenarios: port scan → flow or packet evidence; large file transfer → flow plus endpoint context; suspicious DNS domain → DNS/Zeek DNS log plus flow for follow-on traffic. Record one limitation for each.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The exercise reinforces that telemetry should be selected based on the question rather than by habit.

modules.title: Network Protocol Foundations
modules.description: Build packet-reading confidence by moving from Ethernet and IP to transport-layer behavior and reliability clues.

lessons.title: Ethernet, ARP, and Layer-2 Clues
lessons.description: Read Ethernet and ARP behavior that often explains local-network anomalies.
learningObjectives: Identify source/destination MAC addresses and EtherType at a high level.
Recognize ARP request/reply patterns and basic ARP anomalies.

notes.text: Ethernet frames provide local-link context before an IP packet is interpreted. ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on a local broadcast domain. In captures, repeated ARP probes, conflicting replies, or a sudden change in the observed MAC for an IP can be investigative clues, although they require corroboration.

items: Broadcast ARP requests commonly ask who owns an IPv4 address.
ARP is local-segment behavior; routers do not forward ARP broadcasts.
Do not equate an ARP anomaly with compromise without checking normal network behavior and device changes.

quiz.question: What does an ARP reply primarily associate?
options: IPv4 address with a MAC address
quiz.answer: IPv4 address with a MAC address
quiz.explanation: ARP is used on IPv4 local networks to discover the MAC address associated with an IPv4 address.

summary: Ethernet frames provide local-link context before an IP packet is interpreted. ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on a local broadcast domain. In captures, repeated ARP probes, conflicting replies, or a sudden change in the observed MAC for an IP can be investigative clues, although they require corroboration.

lessons.title: IPv4, IPv6, and Routing Evidence
lessons.description: Interpret IP headers and route-related context without overfitting to addresses alone.
learningObjectives: Interpret source/destination IPs, TTL/hop-limit, protocol, and fragmentation indicators.
Use subnet and routing context to distinguish local, internal, and external traffic.

notes.text: IP metadata gives direction and addressing context. TTL in IPv4 and Hop Limit in IPv6 decreases as packets traverse routers, making it useful as a clue but not a reliable fingerprint by itself. Fragmentation can complicate reassembly and filtering, so analysts should note when packets are incomplete or fragmented.

IPv4 quick fields: src, dst, ttl, protocol, total_length
IPv6 quick fields: src, dst, hop_limit, next_header, payload_length

quiz.question: Which field identifies the transport or upper-layer protocol carried by IPv4?
quiz.answer: Protocol
quiz.explanation: The IPv4 Protocol field identifies the next protocol, such as TCP, UDP, or ICMP.

summary: IP metadata gives direction and addressing context. TTL in IPv4 and Hop Limit in IPv6 decreases as packets traverse routers, making it useful as a clue but not a reliable fingerprint by itself. Fragmentation can complicate reassembly and filtering, so analysts should note when packets are incomplete or fragmented.

lessons.title: TCP Deep Dive: Three-Way Handshake
lessons.description: Understand SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, ports, sequence numbers, and connection establishment.
learningObjectives: Trace a normal TCP three-way handshake.
Identify half-open attempts, resets, and handshake failures in captures.

notes.text: TCP provides a reliable byte-stream service. Connection establishment commonly uses SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK. Sequence and acknowledgment numbers are central to tracking bytes. A burst of SYNs without completed handshakes can be a symptom of scanning or service stress, but analysts should compare with expected traffic and server-side evidence.

Client → Server: SYN
Server → Client: SYN, ACK
Client → Server: ACK

quiz.question: Which packet completes the standard three-way TCP handshake?
quiz.answer: ACK
quiz.explanation: The client acknowledges the server’s SYN-ACK with an ACK, completing the common handshake sequence.

summary: TCP provides a reliable byte-stream service. Connection establishment commonly uses SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK. Sequence and acknowledgment numbers are central to tracking bytes. A burst of SYNs without completed handshakes can be a symptom of scanning or service stress, but analysts should compare with expected traffic and server-side evidence.

lessons.title: TCP Reliability, Retransmissions, and Resets
lessons.description: Differentiate loss, congestion, application behavior, and abrupt termination.
learningObjectives: Recognize retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, out-of-order packets, and RSTs.
Avoid labeling every retransmission as malicious or every RST as an attack.

notes.text: TCP analysis frequently requires sequence-aware reasoning. Retransmissions may arise from packet loss or timing issues; duplicate acknowledgments can indicate missing data; RST closes a connection abruptly. Wireshark’s TCP analysis flags are useful hints, but they are interpretations built from the observed trace and should be checked against the capture environment.

items: Look at direction, timing, sequence numbers, and packet loss together.
A reset can be sent by an application, kernel, firewall, or intermediary depending on path and policy.
Correlate with server logs when possible.

quiz.question: Why should a retransmission not automatically be classified as an attack indicator?
options: Retransmissions can occur during normal loss or congestion
quiz.answer: Retransmissions can occur during normal loss or congestion
quiz.explanation: Loss, congestion, and path conditions can produce retransmissions without malicious intent.

summary: TCP analysis frequently requires sequence-aware reasoning. Retransmissions may arise from packet loss or timing issues; duplicate acknowledgments can indicate missing data; RST closes a connection abruptly. Wireshark’s TCP analysis flags are useful hints, but they are interpretations built from the observed trace and should be checked against the capture environment.

tasks.title: Reconstruct a TCP Handshake
tasks.description: Analyze a supplied capture and annotate a complete TCP connection establishment.
tasks.problemStatement: Identify the client/server 4-tuple, locate SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK, and note any handshake failures or resets nearby.
tasks.hint: Use tcp.flags and follow the stream only after identifying the connection.
tasks.solutionCode: Use display filter tcp, identify the SYN packet without ACK, match the reversed tuple SYN-ACK, then the final ACK. If absent, record the handshake as incomplete and investigate retransmissions or resets.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The student should produce a short evidence table rather than a binary “good/bad” verdict.

modules.title: UDP, ICMP, and DNS Analysis
modules.description: Learn the most common stateless protocols and build reliable reasoning around DNS as a primary network pivot.

lessons.title: UDP and Stateless Conversation Patterns
lessons.description: Analyze UDP traffic as request/response or one-way datagrams without TCP session semantics.
learningObjectives: Explain what UDP does not guarantee compared with TCP.
Recognize UDP request/response patterns and common diagnostic pitfalls.

notes.text: UDP is a minimal datagram transport. It does not provide TCP-style connection establishment, retransmission, or ordering guarantees. Analysts often infer an application exchange from timing and matching source/destination fields rather than a formal session handshake.

items: DNS commonly uses UDP, but other transports can be used when needed.
A missing UDP response is not automatically a dropped packet; the server may have rejected, rate-limited, or simply not answered.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes UDP?
options: It provides a datagram service without guaranteed delivery
quiz.answer: It provides a datagram service without guaranteed delivery
quiz.explanation: RFC 768 defines UDP as a minimal transaction-oriented datagram protocol without guaranteed delivery or duplicate protection.

summary: UDP is a minimal datagram transport. It does not provide TCP-style connection establishment, retransmission, or ordering guarantees. Analysts often infer an application exchange from timing and matching source/destination fields rather than a formal session handshake.

lessons.title: ICMP and Reachability Analysis
lessons.description: Use ICMP types and timing to reason about reachability, errors, and network troubleshooting.
learningObjectives: Recognize common ICMP echo and unreachable behavior.
Separate reachability evidence from security conclusions.

notes.text: ICMP communicates network-layer control and error information. Echo request/reply is often used for reachability tests, while unreachable messages can indicate routing or filtering conditions. ICMP observations are contextual: a host can be reachable over one protocol while another service is blocked.

items: Ping success proves a particular ICMP path works, not that an application is healthy.
ICMP may be filtered or rate-limited, so absence of reply is ambiguous.

quiz.question: What does a successful ICMP echo reply demonstrate most directly?
quiz.answer: A specific ICMP exchange completed
quiz.explanation: Echo reply is evidence that the corresponding ICMP exchange succeeded, not proof of application availability.

summary: ICMP communicates network-layer control and error information. Echo request/reply is often used for reachability tests, while unreachable messages can indicate routing or filtering conditions. ICMP observations are contextual: a host can be reachable over one protocol while another service is blocked.

lessons.title: DNS Transactions and Resolver Behavior
lessons.description: Trace DNS queries, responses, record types, response codes, and resolver relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify DNS client/server roles, query names, types, and response codes.
Explain why resolver telemetry can be more informative than raw destination IPs alone.

notes.text: DNS translates names to records and often acts as a key pivot for traffic analysis. Analysts should record the querying host, resolver, queried name, record type, response code, answer values, and timing. Zeek’s dns.log exposes many of these fields in structured form.
Common DNS fields: query, qtype, rcode, answers, id.orig_h, id.resp_h, ts

quiz.question: Which field in a DNS record tells you the requested record type, such as A or AAAA?
quiz.answer: qtype
quiz.explanation: The query type identifies what record type the client requested.

summary: DNS translates names to records and often acts as a key pivot for traffic analysis. Analysts should record the querying host, resolver, queried name, record type, response code, answer values, and timing. Zeek’s dns.log exposes many of these fields in structured form.

lessons.title: DNS Abuse Clues and Analytical Limits
lessons.description: Study suspicious-domain, tunneling, fast-flux-like, and high-entropy clues while avoiding overclaiming.
learningObjectives: Use DNS frequency, entropy-like properties, and response patterns as hypotheses.
Combine DNS evidence with follow-on connections and asset context.

notes.text: Suspicious DNS behavior can include unusually long labels, high query volume, many unique subdomains, rare destinations, or short-lived infrastructure. None is conclusive alone. Legitimate CDNs, software update systems, security tooling, and telemetry services can produce similarly unusual patterns.
Do not treat a long or random-looking DNS label as proof of tunneling. Validate with volume, destination behavior, timing, known software, and endpoint context.

quiz.question: Why is DNS-based suspicion strongest when correlated with other telemetry?
options: Similar DNS patterns can be produced by benign systems
quiz.answer: Similar DNS patterns can be produced by benign systems
quiz.explanation: Many legitimate services use dynamic names, CDNs, or telemetry subdomains, so correlation reduces false positives.

summary: Suspicious DNS behavior can include unusually long labels, high query volume, many unique subdomains, rare destinations, or short-lived infrastructure. None is conclusive alone. Legitimate CDNs, software update systems, security tooling, and telemetry services can produce similarly unusual patterns.

tasks.title: DNS Triage Worksheet
tasks.description: Turn DNS observations into an evidence-based hypothesis.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a list of DNS query metadata, identify unusual query volume, rare names, and follow-on destination patterns, then state two benign explanations and two malicious hypotheses.
requirements: Spreadsheet, Python, or shell tooling; synthetic DNS dataset.
tasks.hint: Start with per-host query count, unique domains, and unique destination IPs before inspecting strings.
tasks.solutionCode: For each source host, compute count, unique query count, and unique destination count; flag outliers; then inspect whether the flagged domains lead to consistent external connections. Explicitly separate “suspicious” from “confirmed malicious.”
tasks.solutionExplanation: The expected result is a ranked analyst hypothesis with supporting and contradictory evidence.

modules.title: HTTP, TLS, and Modern Web Traffic
modules.description: Move from raw packet fields to application-layer reasoning, encrypted-traffic limitations, and modern QUIC-based web visibility.

lessons.title: HTTP Request and Response Anatomy
lessons.description: Interpret HTTP methods, hosts, status codes, headers, content lengths, and timing.
learningObjectives: Identify key HTTP request and response fields in packet captures.
Use HTTP metadata to reconstruct a high-level transaction timeline.

notes.text: HTTP exposes application semantics that often make packet analysis much easier when payloads are visible. Analysts can correlate request method, host, URI, status code, response size, and timing. Even without payloads, these fields can sometimes survive in sensor logs or proxies.

items: GET/POST describe common request intent, not necessarily benign/malicious purpose.
Host and URI should be analyzed with destination, user-agent, and timing context.
Large responses and repeated requests are hypotheses, not verdicts.

quiz.question: Which HTTP response element is most directly used to indicate whether a request succeeded at the application layer?
quiz.answer: Status code
quiz.explanation: HTTP status codes communicate the response outcome category, such as success, redirection, client error, or server error.

summary: HTTP exposes application semantics that often make packet analysis much easier when payloads are visible. Analysts can correlate request method, host, URI, status code, response size, and timing. Even without payloads, these fields can sometimes survive in sensor logs or proxies.

lessons.title: TLS Handshake and Metadata
lessons.description: Understand ClientHello, ServerHello, certificates, SNI/related metadata, and the limits of encrypted payload visibility.
learningObjectives: Identify the major stages of a modern TLS handshake at a conceptual level.
Extract useful metadata without claiming access to encrypted content.

notes.text: TLS encrypts application data, but the handshake still exposes useful metadata depending on protocol version, deployment, and visibility point. Analysts commonly inspect the client/server addresses, handshake timing, certificate context, negotiated parameters, and available hostname metadata. Encryption reduces content visibility; it does not eliminate network evidence.
Never infer exact application behavior from a destination IP alone when TLS is in use. CDN and shared-hosting infrastructure can host many unrelated services.

quiz.question: What is the analyst’s most important limitation when inspecting standard TLS-protected application traffic?
options: Application payloads are generally not readable from the capture alone
quiz.answer: Application payloads are generally not readable from the capture alone
quiz.explanation: TLS protects application payloads, so packet analysis shifts toward metadata, endpoints, timing, certificates, and corroborating telemetry.

summary: TLS encrypts application data, but the handshake still exposes useful metadata depending on protocol version, deployment, and visibility point. Analysts commonly inspect the client/server addresses, handshake timing, certificate context, negotiated parameters, and available hostname metadata. Encryption reduces content visibility; it does not eliminate network evidence.

lessons.title: QUIC and HTTP/3 Visibility
lessons.description: Recognize QUIC over UDP and understand why transport analysis differs from TCP-based HTTPS.
learningObjectives: Identify QUIC traffic patterns and the role of UDP.
Explain why TCP-centric filters miss HTTP/3 traffic.

notes.text: QUIC runs over UDP and provides transport features such as reliable streams and connection management above UDP. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, so analysts need UDP-aware tooling and protocol support. This matters operationally because a monitor designed around TCP/443 alone can undercount modern web traffic.

items: Look for UDP flows commonly associated with QUIC, but avoid relying solely on port numbers.
Use protocol-aware dissectors or sensor logs when available.

quiz.question: Why can a monitoring rule limited to tcp.port == 443 miss some modern web traffic?
options: Because HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP
quiz.answer: Because HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP
quiz.explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which runs over UDP, so TCP-only filters can miss it.

summary: QUIC runs over UDP and provides transport features such as reliable streams and connection management above UDP. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, so analysts need UDP-aware tooling and protocol support. This matters operationally because a monitor designed around TCP/443 alone can undercount modern web traffic.

lessons.title: User-Agent, Content, and Behavioral Clues
lessons.description: Use application metadata and timing patterns to form hypotheses about clients, downloads, automation, and anomalies.
learningObjectives: Compare client metadata across HTTP observations.
Identify behavioral clues that deserve endpoint or reputation checks.

notes.text: User-Agent strings, request cadence, response sizes, and content types can distinguish browsers, scripted clients, update agents, and unusual automation. These fields are mutable and can be forged, so they should be used as context rather than identity proof.

items: Rare user agents may warrant inspection when paired with unusual destination or request behavior.
Repeated small requests can indicate API polling; repeated large responses may indicate synchronization or downloads.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of using User-Agent as an identity signal?
options: It can be changed by the client
quiz.answer: It can be changed by the client
quiz.explanation: User-Agent is client-supplied metadata and can be customized or spoofed.

summary: User-Agent strings, request cadence, response sizes, and content types can distinguish browsers, scripted clients, update agents, and unusual automation. These fields are mutable and can be forged, so they should be used as context rather than identity proof.

tasks.title: Encrypted Web Traffic Triage
tasks.description: Investigate suspicious HTTPS without decrypting payloads.
tasks.problemStatement: From synthetic connection metadata, rank three destinations using SNI/certificate context, JA3-like or fingerprint-style fields if available, timing, byte counts, and asset role.
objectives: Separate infrastructure reputation from traffic behavior.
requirements: Synthetic TLS/flow dataset; spreadsheet or Python.
tasks.hint: Do not make reputation the only signal; examine periodicity, volume, and destination prevalence.
tasks.solutionCode: Create a scoring table where each signal contributes evidence, then write a narrative explaining why the top-ranked flow deserves deeper review and what additional telemetry is needed.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A ranked shortlist plus explicit data gaps.

modules.title: Wireshark and TShark Practice
modules.description: Build practical packet-analysis workflows using filters, stream reconstruction, and CLI extraction.

lessons.title: Wireshark Workspace and Packet Dissection
lessons.description: Learn the core Wireshark views used during packet-level investigations.
learningObjectives: Navigate packet list, packet details, and packet bytes.
Move between protocol layers without losing the original packet context.

notes.text: Wireshark provides a packet list, a structured protocol tree, and raw bytes. A strong workflow starts broad, narrows with filters, then inspects a small number of packets in context. Analysts should record the exact filter and packet scope used so another person can reproduce the observation.

items: Coloring rules are visual aids, not evidence by themselves.
Packet comments and saved display filters improve repeatability.

quiz.question: Which Wireshark view exposes decoded protocol fields as a tree?
quiz.answer: Packet details pane
quiz.explanation: The packet details pane presents decoded protocol fields hierarchically.

summary: Wireshark provides a packet list, a structured protocol tree, and raw bytes. A strong workflow starts broad, narrows with filters, then inspects a small number of packets in context. Analysts should record the exact filter and packet scope used so another person can reproduce the observation.

lessons.title: Capture Filters vs Display Filters
lessons.description: Understand when a filter controls collection versus presentation.
learningObjectives: Distinguish capture-filter syntax from display-filter syntax.
Choose the safer point to apply filtering for a given use case.

notes.text: Capture filters constrain what is collected and can reduce volume before packets are written. Display filters act after capture and determine which packets are shown. The syntaxes differ, so analysts must not assume one can be substituted for the other.

Example display filters:
ip.addr == 192.0.2.10
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0
dns

practicals.title: Filter a PCAP by TCP Handshake State
practicals.description: Use Wireshark to isolate initial TCP SYN packets and compare them with completed handshakes in an authorized capture.
steps: Open the authorized PCAP in Wireshark.
Apply `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0` as a display filter.
Record source/destination addresses and ports.
Clear the filter and identify SYN-ACK and final ACK packets.
Document one complete handshake and one incomplete attempt if present.
practicals.solution: Use the filter `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`, then follow the four-tuple to identify the related SYN-ACK and client ACK. Record packet numbers and timestamps.
practicals.output: A traceable handshake annotation and a short evidence table.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Capture filters and display filters use identical syntax
Display filters control which captured packets are shown
Display filters prevent packets from being captured
Capture filters only work after capture
quiz.answer: Display filters control which captured packets are shown
quiz.explanation: Wireshark documentation describes capture filters as capture-time constraints and display filters as view-time expressions.

summary: Capture filters constrain what is collected and can reduce volume before packets are written. Display filters act after capture and determine which packets are shown. The syntaxes differ, so analysts must not assume one can be substituted for the other.

lessons.title: Following Conversations and Streams
lessons.description: Reconstruct a conversation, inspect directionality, and avoid being misled by a single packet.
learningObjectives: Use stream/conversation views to pivot from a packet to related traffic.
Explain why stream reconstruction is useful for application-level context.

notes.text: A single packet rarely answers an investigation. Conversation tables, Follow TCP Stream, and endpoint statistics let analysts pivot from one packet to the surrounding exchange. Stream reconstruction should be combined with timestamps, retransmission analysis, and the full capture boundaries.

items: Record the stream index or flow identifiers when documenting evidence.
Check both directions before drawing conclusions from one side of a conversation.

quiz.question: Why is following a TCP stream often more useful than inspecting one packet?
options: It reconstructs the broader byte exchange
quiz.answer: It reconstructs the broader byte exchange
quiz.explanation: Following a stream groups related packets so the analyst can inspect the sequence of the conversation.

summary: A single packet rarely answers an investigation. Conversation tables, Follow TCP Stream, and endpoint statistics let analysts pivot from one packet to the surrounding exchange. Stream reconstruction should be combined with timestamps, retransmission analysis, and the full capture boundaries.

lessons.title: TShark for Repeatable CLI Analysis
lessons.description: Use TShark to read captures, filter packets, and extract fields into pipelines.
learningObjectives: Run TShark against saved PCAP/pcapng files.
Extract protocol fields suitable for repeatable scripts and reports.

notes.text: TShark is Wireshark’s command-line protocol analyzer. It is especially useful when analysts need repeatable extraction across many captures. The -r option reads a saved capture; display filters can select packets, and field extraction can produce machine-readable output for scripting.

tshark -r sample.pcapng -Y "dns"
tshark -r sample.pcapng -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0"

quiz.question: Which TShark option reads an existing capture file?
quiz.answer: -r
quiz.explanation: The TShark manual documents -r for reading a capture file.

summary: TShark is Wireshark’s command-line protocol analyzer. It is especially useful when analysts need repeatable extraction across many captures. The -r option reads a saved capture; display filters can select packets, and field extraction can produce machine-readable output for scripting.

tasks.title: Create a Reproducible TShark Extractor
tasks.description: Extract DNS and TCP handshake indicators from a PCAP using a repeatable shell command set.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a small report containing packet number, timestamp, source/destination IP, transport protocol, and DNS query or SYN state where relevant.
tasks.hint: Start with `-Y` filters, then add field extraction only after the filter is correct.
tasks.solutionCode:
Example approach:
`tshark -r sample.pcapng -Y "dns" -T fields -e frame.number -e frame.time_epoch -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e dns.qry.name`
For SYNs use `-Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0"` and appropriate TCP fields.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A reproducible command transcript and CSV-like output suitable for later analysis.

learningObjectives: Explain Zeek’s role in producing structured network logs.

notes.text: Zeek transforms observed traffic into structured logs representing connections and protocol events. It can process live traffic or stored captures.

items: Zeek logs are evidence derived from traffic, not raw packets.

quiz.question: What is Zeek best known for in a network-analysis workflow?
options: Generating structured network telemetry from observed traffic
quiz.answer: Generating structured network telemetry from observed traffic

lessons.title: conn.log and Network Conversation Summaries

Group records by `id.orig_h`.

lessons.title: Suricata Detection Model
lessons.description: Understand signatures, alerts, protocol metadata, and the role of Suricata in NSM/IDS workflows.
learningObjectives: Explain how Suricata uses rules and protocol inspection.
Differentiate an IDS alert from proof of successful compromise.

notes.text: Suricata combines packet processing, protocol analysis, and rules to generate alerts and structured events. An alert indicates that observed traffic matched a detection condition; it does not by itself prove exploit success, persistence, or intent.
Treat IDS alerts as leads. Validate source/destination context, timing, asset role, and related telemetry before escalating.

quiz.question: What does a Suricata alert most directly prove?
options: Observed traffic matched a detection condition
quiz.answer: Observed traffic matched a detection condition

lessons.title: EVE JSON Structure
lessons.description: Read Suricata EVE JSON alert and protocol events as structured telemetry.
learningObjectives: Identify common EVE JSON top-level fields.
Parse event_type-specific fields without assuming every record has the same schema.

{"timestamp":"...","event_type":"alert", "src_ip":"...", "dest_ip":"...", "alert":{...}}

practicals.title: Parse Suricata EVE Alerts
practicals.description: Extract alert records from Suricata EVE JSON and summarize recurring signatures.
steps: Prepare an authorized or synthetic eve.json file.
Read one JSON object per line.
Keep only `event_type == "alert"`.
Extract signature and endpoints.
Count signatures and inspect recurring rules.

Different event types expose different schemas
It contains the TCP sequence number

lessons.title: Writing and Tuning Suricata Rules
lessons.description: Design rule logic that is specific, testable, and resistant to obvious noise.
learningObjectives: Explain rule action, protocol, direction, addresses, ports, and content conditions.
Use context and false-positive analysis to tune a rule.

notes.text: A useful Suricata rule expresses a concrete detection hypothesis. Start with the narrowest observable that maps to the behavior you care about, then add protocol, direction, and context constraints. Tuning should be based on representative benign traffic as well as known-positive tests.

action protocol src_addr src_port -> dst_addr dst_port (msg:"..."; content:"..."; sid:1000001;)

quiz.question: What is the best first step when a rule fires too often?
options: Inspect representative false positives and refine the detection logic
quiz.answer: Inspect representative false positives and refine the detection logic
quiz.explanation: Tuning should be evidence-driven: inspect why benign traffic matches and change the conditions that create the ambiguity.

summary: A useful Suricata rule expresses a concrete detection hypothesis. Start with the narrowest observable that maps to the behavior you care about, then add protocol, direction, and context constraints. Tuning should be based on representative benign traffic as well as known-positive tests.

lessons.title: Alert Correlation and Validation
lessons.description: Correlate IDS alerts with packet and flow evidence before assigning severity.
learningObjectives: Validate alerts with surrounding packet context.
Explain how duplicate or chained alerts can be normalized during triage.

notes.text: A single network event can trigger several signatures or produce repeated alerts. Correlation can reduce analyst fatigue by grouping events around a connection, source/destination pair, rule family, and time window. items: Compare alert time with the first packet and connection duration.
Look for preceding DNS and following connections to understand the wider sequence.

options: To prove every alert is malicious
To understand whether the alert is isolated, repeated, or part of a larger behavior
quiz.answer: To understand whether the alert is isolated, repeated, or part of a larger behavior
quiz.explanation: Correlation adds context and can distinguish one-off matches from sustained or chained activity.

summary: A single network event can trigger several signatures or produce repeated alerts. Correlation can reduce analyst fatigue by grouping events around a connection, source/destination pair, rule family, and time window. The goal is to preserve the raw evidence while presenting a normalized investigation unit.

tasks.title: Tune a Noisy IDS Rule
tasks.description: Reduce false positives without losing the intended behavior.
tasks.problemStatement: Given synthetic alert examples and benign traffic context, refine a detection rule so routine software updates no longer trigger while the suspicious pattern remains detectable.
requirements: Suricata rule syntax; synthetic test traffic or rule test data.
tasks.hint: Prefer constraints grounded in protocol behavior or asset context over arbitrary IP exclusions.
tasks.solutionCode: Document the original rule, example false positives, the refined rule, and why each changed condition narrows the match. Include a test case that still triggers the refined rule.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A before/after rule comparison with explicit validation cases.

lessons.title: Flow Records and 5-Tuple Reasoning
lessons.description: Analyze NetFlow/IPFIX/VPC-flow style metadata without packets.
learningObjectives: Explain the value and limitations of flow records.
Use 5-tuple, bytes, packets, duration, and action fields for triage.

Cloud flow logs add provider-specific fields and do not represent packet payloads.

items: Flow records are excellent for volume and direction analysis.
Sampling or aggregation can hide short or low-volume events.
Provider flow logs may be delivered asynchronously and should not be treated as packet-by-packet timelines.

quiz.question: What is a major blind spot of flow records?
options: They usually lack application payload content
quiz.answer: They usually lack application payload content
quiz.explanation: Flow records are metadata summaries; payload-level evidence requires packet capture or other application telemetry.

summary: Flow telemetry summarizes network conversations and is often cheaper to retain than raw packet captures. lessons.title: Baselining and Percentiles
lessons.description: Build baselines for destination counts, bytes, ports, and connection frequency without relying on arbitrary thresholds.
learningObjectives: Use distributions and percentiles for network baselines.
Explain why a single global threshold can be misleading.

notes.text: Baselining turns “unusual” into a measurable deviation from a relevant peer group. A database server and a developer workstation should not share the same normal profile. Percentiles are often more robust than fixed limits when traffic volume varies significantly across assets or time windows.
Conceptual baseline: threshold = percentile(metric, 99) within peer group and time window

quiz.question: Why is a peer-group baseline usually better than one threshold for every host?
options: Different roles have different expected traffic patterns
quiz.answer: Different roles have different expected traffic patterns
quiz.explanation: Role-aware baselines reduce false positives by comparing an asset with similar systems.

summary: Baselining turns “unusual” into a measurable deviation from a relevant peer group. A database server and a developer workstation should not share the same normal profile. lessons.title: Scanning and Service Discovery Patterns
lessons.description: Detect scanning behavior using destination breadth, sequential probing, and time windows.
learningObjectives: Describe flow-based indicators of scanning.
Implement a simple unique-destination/port window analysis.

notes.text: Scanning can manifest as one source contacting many destinations or many ports in a short period. MITRE ATT&CK’s Network Service Discovery technique and detection strategies emphasize correlating network connection activity with process or network telemetry rather than relying on a single packet pattern.

Conceptual metric:
unique_destinations(src, 5m)
unique_ports(src, 5m)
probe_rate = attempts / minute

practicals.title: Detect a Small Scan in Flow Data
practicals.description: Identify a source that contacts many destinations in a short time window.
steps: Create a CSV with timestamp, source, destination, and destination port.
Normalize timestamps to UTC.
Group rows by source.
Evaluate five-minute windows.
Review candidates against known administrative activity.
practicals.solution: For each source, sort events by time; build five-minute windows; calculate unique destinations and ports; flag windows meeting the selected threshold; preserve the window start and counts.
practicals.output: A ranked list of scan candidates with supporting counts.

quiz.question: Which observation most strongly suggests horizontal scanning?
options: One host makes one DNS query
One source contacts many unique destination IPs in a short window
A host opens a single SSH connection
quiz.answer: One source contacts many unique destination IPs in a short window
quiz.explanation: Horizontal scanning targets multiple hosts; breadth across destination IPs is a key signal.

summary: Scanning can manifest as one source contacting many destinations or many ports in a short period. MITRE ATT&CK’s Network Service Discovery technique and detection strategies emphasize correlating network connection activity with process or network telemetry rather than relying on a single packet pattern.

lessons.title: Beaconing, Periodicity, and Long-Running Sessions
lessons.description: Analyze repeated outbound communications and distinguish periodic behavior from ordinary scheduled activity.
learningObjectives: Measure inter-arrival times for repeated connections.
Combine periodicity with destination rarity, bytes, and asset role.

notes.text: Beacon-like traffic can exhibit regular intervals, low byte counts, long duration patterns, or repeated destination targeting. items: Look for low variance in inter-arrival times across multiple observations.
Test whether the same pattern appears across known-benign peers.

quiz.question: Why is periodicity alone insufficient to classify beaconing as malicious?
options: Scheduled services can also be periodic
quiz.answer: Scheduled services can also be periodic
quiz.explanation: Many legitimate systems communicate on timers, so context and corroboration are required.

summary: Beacon-like traffic can exhibit regular intervals, low byte counts, long duration patterns, or repeated destination targeting. tasks.title: Detect a Scan from Flow Data
tasks.description: Build a sliding-window scan detector using synthetic flow records.
tasks.problemStatement: Flag sources that contact at least 20 unique destinations or 20 unique destination ports within five minutes, then tune the threshold using known administrative scanner activity.
objectives: Whitelist authorized scanner assets based on context.
tasks.hint: Keep the raw data and produce a second field explaining why a row/window was flagged.
tasks.solutionCode: Implement a five-minute sliding window grouped by source. Calculate unique destination IPs/ports and compare to the chosen threshold. Exclude explicitly documented authorized scanner addresses from the alert output, while still recording that they were observed.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A detector report containing flagged windows, source, counts, and tuning notes.

modules.title: Encrypted and Cloud Network Analysis

lessons.title: Encrypted Traffic Without Decryption

learningObjectives: Identify useful fields available without payload decryption.
State the confidence and limitations of encrypted-traffic inferences.

notes.text: When payloads are encrypted, analysts can still inspect endpoints, ports, timing, packet sizes, directionality, handshake metadata, certificates, DNS, and flow patterns. These signals support probabilistic conclusions, not exact content reconstruction.

items: Start from asset role and expected destination categories.
Compare suspicious traffic with historical behavior from the same host.
Use endpoint telemetry when network evidence is insufficient.

lessons.title: Certificates and TLS Trust Context

learningObjectives: Explain what a certificate can reveal and what it cannot.

items: Compare certificate subject/SAN context with DNS names and destination infrastructure.
Check time validity against the observed timestamp.

Use certificate names and reuse as a pivot for related observations
Assume every shared certificate belongs to one organization
quiz.answer: Use certificate names and reuse as a pivot for related observations

summary: TLS certificates can contain names, issuers, validity windows, public-key parameters, and chain information. Shared certificates can appear across hosted services, so certificate reuse is useful as a pivot but not proof of common ownership or maliciousness.

lessons.title: Traffic Classification and Fingerprinting Limits
lessons.description: Understand statistical and protocol fingerprints while avoiding brittle attribution claims.

options: Different applications can share or change observable characteristics

lessons.title: Cloud Flow Telemetry and Shared Infrastructure

Shared services and load balancers can host multiple applications

tasks.title: Build an Encrypted-Traffic Evidence Matrix

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK-Aligned Network Detections

code.network_traffic_tool.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Local, offline network-traffic triage toolkit.

Input: JSON Lines records with fields:
  time, src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port, proto,
  bytes, packets, event_type, domain, signature

The tool produces explainable scan, beacon, and rare-destination findings.
It does not capture live traffic or perform active scanning.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import collections
import datetime as dt
import json
import math
import statistics
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Iterable


def parse_time(value: str) -> dt.datetime:
    value = value.strip()
    if value.endswith("Z"):
        value = value[:-1] + "+00:00"
    parsed = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(value)
    if parsed.tzinfo is None:
        parsed = parsed.replace(tzinfo=dt.timezone.utc)
    return parsed.astimezone(dt.timezone.utc)


def load_events(path: Path) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    events: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line_no, line in enumerate(handle, 1):
            if not line.strip():
                continue
            try:
                obj = json.loads(line)
                required = ["time", "src_ip", "dst_ip", "src_port", "dst_port", "proto"]
                missing = [k for k in required if k not in obj]
                if missing:
                    raise ValueError(f"missing fields: {', '.join(missing)}")
                obj["_time"] = parse_time(str(obj["time"]))
                obj["bytes"] = int(obj.get("bytes", 0) or 0)
                obj["packets"] = int(obj.get("packets", 0) or 0)
                obj["src_port"] = int(obj["src_port"])
                obj["dst_port"] = int(obj["dst_port"])
                events.append(obj)
            except (ValueError, TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
                print(f"WARN line {line_no}: {exc}")
    return sorted(events, key=lambda e: e["_time"])


def scan_findings(events: list[dict[str, Any]], window_seconds: int = 300,
                  dest_threshold: int = 8, port_threshold: int = 8) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    by_src: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]] = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for event in events:
        by_src[event["src_ip"]].append(event)
    findings: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for src, rows in by_src.items():
        left = 0
        for right, current in enumerate(rows):
            while (current["_time"] - rows[left]["_time"]).total_seconds() > window_seconds:
                left += 1
            bucket = rows[left:right + 1]
            unique_dests = sorted({r["dst_ip"] for r in bucket})
            unique_ports = sorted({r["dst_port"] for r in bucket})
            if len(unique_dests) >= dest_threshold or len(unique_ports) >= port_threshold:
                findings.append({
                    "type": "scan",
                    "src_ip": src,
                    "window_start": bucket[0]["_time"].isoformat(),
                    "window_end": current["_time"].isoformat(),
                    "unique_destinations": len(unique_dests),
                    "unique_ports": len(unique_ports),
                    "evidence": "breadth exceeds configured threshold"
                })
                break
    return findings


def beacon_findings(events: list[dict[str, Any]], min_points: int = 5,
                    max_cv: float = 0.15) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    grouped: dict[tuple[str, str, int], list[dt.datetime]] = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for e in events:
        grouped[(e["src_ip"], e["dst_ip"], e["dst_port"])].append(e["_time"])
    findings = []
    for (src, dst, port), times in grouped.items():
        times.sort()
        if len(times) < min_points:
            continue
        intervals = [(b - a).total_seconds() for a, b in zip(times, times[1:])]
        mean = statistics.mean(intervals)
        if mean <= 0:
            continue
        stdev = statistics.pstdev(intervals)
        cv = stdev / mean
        if cv <= max_cv:
            findings.append({
                "type": "periodic",
                "src_ip": src,
                "dst_ip": dst,
                "dst_port": port,
                "observations": len(times),
                "mean_interval_seconds": round(mean, 3),
                "coefficient_variation": round(cv, 4),
                "evidence": "low variance in inter-arrival times"
            })
    return findings


def rarity_findings(events: list[dict[str, Any]], top_n: int = 10) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    counts = collections.Counter(e["dst_ip"] for e in events)
    findings = []
    for e in events:
        if counts[e["dst_ip"]] == 1:
            findings.append({
                "type": "rare_destination",
                "time": e["_time"].isoformat(),
                "src_ip": e["src_ip"],
                "dst_ip": e["dst_ip"],
                "dst_port": e["dst_port"],
                "domain": e.get("domain"),
                "evidence": "destination observed once in supplied dataset"
            })
    return findings[:top_n]


def print_report(events: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
    if not events:
        print("No valid events loaded.")
        return
    print(f"Loaded events: {len(events)}")
    print(f"Time range: {events[0]['_time'].isoformat()} -> {events[-1]['_time'].isoformat()}")
    scans = scan_findings(events)
    beacons = beacon_findings(events)
    rare = rarity_findings(events)
    print(f"Scan findings: {len(scans)}")
    for item in scans:
        print(json.dumps(item, sort_keys=True))
    print(f"Periodic findings: {len(beacons)}")
    for item in beacons:
        print(json.dumps(item, sort_keys=True))
    print(f"Rare-destination findings: {len(rare)}")
    for item in rare:
        print(json.dumps(item, sort_keys=True))


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Offline network-traffic triage")
    parser.add_argument("input", type=Path, help="JSONL network event file")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    events = load_events(args.input)
    print_report(events)
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

project.explanation: The toolkit models a small but defensible network-analysis pipeline. `load_events` validates and normalizes input timestamps while retaining malformed-row warnings. `scan_findings` uses a five-minute sliding window per source and counts unique destination IPs and ports to identify breadth. `beacon_findings` groups traffic by source, destination, and port and computes the coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times; low variance indicates periodicity but is intentionally not labeled as malicious. `rarity_findings` highlights destinations seen only once in the supplied dataset. Each finding includes the observations that caused the heuristic to fire. The analyst must then review context, asset role, expected software, and additional telemetry before making an incident decision. The project therefore demonstrates a complete network-analysis loop: source data → normalization → explainable detection → human validation → documented conclusion.
